beats: You got a two-thousand-dollar raise. Now someone warns you: higher tax bracket.
The myth? That the higher rate hits your whole salary.
Canada uses marginal rates. Each rate only taxes its own slice.
Say your taxable income is sixty thousand. The first fifty-eight thousand, five hundred twenty-three is taxed federally at fourteen percent.
Only the last one thousand, four hundred seventy-seven pays twenty point five.
Real example: Manitoba, twenty twenty-six. Salary from fifty-eight to sixty thousand.
Federal: three eighteen. Manitoba: two thirty-eight. C.P.P. and E.I.: one fifty-two.
You keep one thousand, two hundred and ninety-two dollars. More money. Not less.
One exception: the Canada Child Benefit starts shrinking once family net income passes about thirty-eight thousand.
On benefits? Run the numbers with a pro.
A higher bracket never taxes your whole income.
